texto:
Meet bili. Four letters. At least six jobs. This little word is the chameleon of Gupapuyŋu, and once you know its faces, you'll hear it constantly.

Face 1: already, completion:
Bili ŋarra maḻŋ'maraŋala → I already found it

Face 2: the did-you? question (Lesson 23):
Bili nhe märraŋala? → Did you get it? / Have you got it?
Same word, rising voice. Already + intonation = a perfect question.

Face 3: just, only, the same:
Dhiyaŋu bili walala marrtjina → They went just now
Ŋayi balanya bili → He is the same (balanya = like-this, + bili = exactly so)

Face 4: all the time, with bitjan:
Ŋarra ŋuli djäma bitjan bili → I work all the time
Ŋayi ŋuli buny'tjun bitjan bili → He smokes every day

That bitjan bili tail (literally: doing-thus same) is THE way to say habitually, always, every day. And notice its partner ŋuli, the habitual particle, replacing ga. Together they paint routine: ŋuli says this is a pattern, bitjan bili says and it repeats, same as ever.

Face 5: because (you'll see this properly with the joining words):
Ŋarra rirrikthurruna bili barpuru ŋarra yätjkurru guya ḻuka → I am sick because I ate a bad fish yesterday

So how does one word do all this without chaos? Position and company. Fronted with a question voice → did you? Next to a time word → just. Next to balanya or bitjan → same / as always. Between two clauses → because. The word itself just means something like: complete, settled, that very one. Every face is a shade of doneness.

English scatters this across a dozen words: already, just, same, only, since, because. Gupapuyŋu folds them into one stone and lets the sentence turn it in the light.

Don't memorise the six faces. Just start flagging every bili you meet from now on and asking: which shade of settled is this one? Your ear will sort them faster than any table.
